procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order of the Allahabad High Court, dated September 20, 1965, passed in Criminal Miscellaneous Contempt Application No. 76 of 1964, finding the appellants guilty of contempt of Court, and sentencing each of them to pay a fine of Rs. 500/- and costs.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The second respondent filed a contempt application in the High Court. The High Court held the appellants guilty of contempt of court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order of the Allahabad High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellants, by expelling a party member for filing a suit in court, were guilty of contempt of court.

facts: A member of a political party (the second respondent) filed a lawsuit against another member concerning an internal party election and obtained a temporary injunction.
In response, party officials (the appellants) expelled the member who filed the suit, citing a party resolution that barred members from taking such disputes to court.
One of the appellants then filed an affidavit in court informing it of the expulsion.
As a direct result of the expulsion, the court dismissed the member's injunction application because he was no longer part of the organization.
law: The Supreme Court relied on the legal principle that any conduct which interferes with or prejudices a party to a lawsuit during the litigation constitutes contempt of court.
The Court cited a precedent, *Pratap Singh's Case*, which established this principle.
application: The Court determined that the act of expelling the member and then using that expulsion in the court proceedings was a "deliberate attempt" to interfere with and prejudice the member in the conduct of his lawsuit.

The Court rejected the appellants' defense that they were merely enforcing internal party discipline based on a party resolution. It held that this justification was "no answer" to the charge of contempt, as the effect of their action was to interfere with the judicial process.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that by expelling the member for filing a suit and using that expulsion to undermine his legal proceedings, the appellants' actions interfered with the course of justice. Therefore, the Court held that the appellants were guilty of contempt of court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellants, by expelling a party member for filing a suit in court, were guilty of contempt of court.
appellant_arguments: The expelled member was part of the Congress Organisation and was bound by its rules, regulations, and resolutions.
The appellants were merely acting in accordance with directions from their superiors within the party and were bound to obey those instructions.
The action of expelling the member was based on a resolution of the Congress Working Committee.
The objective of the expulsion was to enforce party discipline, not to interfere with the court proceedings or render the member's suit infructuous.
respondent_arguments: The respondent did not appear in court to present arguments.

cases.principle: Actions taken against a party, such as expulsion from an organization for initiating a lawsuit, which are a deliberate attempt to interfere with the conduct of that litigation, amount to contempt of court.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Taking disciplinary action against a litigant, such as expulsion from an organization, in pursuance of an internal rule that bars members from referring disputes to a court of law, constitutes contempt of court as it is a deliberate attempt to interfere with the conduct of the litigation. It is not a valid defense that such action was taken to enforce internal discipline.
obiter: In view of Article 361, clauses (2) and (3) of the Constitution, contempt proceedings cannot be continued against a party after they have been appointed as a Governor.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The passing of the orders of expulsion by the two appellants against the second respondent, and the filing of a supporting affidavit in the suit by the second appellant, clearly indicated that it was a deliberate attempt by the appellants to interfere with the conduct of the litigation instituted by the second respondent. These acts were of such a nature as to interfere with or prejudice the second respondent in the proceedings connected with his suit.
legal_tests_applied: Whether an action constitutes contempt is determined by whether it directly tends to interfere with pending court proceedings.
If any pressure is put on a party in order to make it act in a particular manner with respect to a pending action, that would amount to contempt of the court in which the matter is pending.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that the expulsion was merely to enforce party discipline was not a valid defense, as the court held: 'It was no answer that the action, by way of expulsion was taken on the basis of the resolution of the party and to enforce discipline in the organisation.'

The court rejected the appellants' claim that their object was not to interfere with the suit, finding instead that their actions constituted a 'deliberate attempt... to interfere with... the conduct of the litigation.'

The court followed its own precedent in Pratap Singh v. Gurbaksh Singh, which found that initiating disciplinary proceedings against a person who had filed a suit amounted to contempt, and it distinguished the English case cited by the appellants.
why_respondent_won: The appellants' actions had a direct and prejudicial effect on the respondent's lawsuit, as the court noted that the respondent's application for a temporary injunction was dismissed substantially because of the expulsion.

The court found that the appellants' conduct—expelling the respondent for filing a suit and then submitting an affidavit to the court about that expulsion—was of a nature that interfered with and prejudiced the respondent's ability to conduct his litigation.

The court's reasoning was in agreement with the majority view in the precedent case of Pratap Singh v. Gurbaksh Singh, which held that similar actions taken against a litigant amounted to contempt of court.
policy_considerations: An organization's internal rules regarding discipline, which bar members from seeking decisions in a court of law, cannot be used to justify actions that interfere with pending litigation, as such conduct is considered 'subversive of discipline' but ultimately amounts to contempt of court.
